strengths: Substantial and impactful dataset contribution: LEMON provides an extensive collection of 4,194 surgical videos across 35 distinct procedures (938 hours, 3.4M frames at 1 fps), significantly advancing open-access data availability beyond existing single-procedure datasets.

Well-designed and systematic data curation pipeline: The multi-stage filtering process—combining storyboard classification, frame trimming, and YOLO-based detection/removal of non-surgical graphics/overlays—effectively addresses web-video noise, as confirmed by the ablation in Table 5.

Intuitive, domain-tailored SSL formulation: The proposed augmented distillation strategy creatively leverages temporal continuity and procedure-level nearest neighbors across patients to induce invariance to intraoperative motion and inter-patient tissue variations.

Comprehensive and convincing empirical validation: Evaluated across six established public benchmarks covering four distinct downstream tasks (surgical phase recognition, tool presence detection, action recognition, and semantic segmentation). LemonFM consistently outperforms specialist methods and existing surgical foundation models (Endo-FM, EndoViT, SurgeNetXL) under linear probing, full fine-tuning, and low-data regimes.
weaknesses: Potential deduplication/leakage concern: Because LEMON is collected from public YouTube uploads, there is a risk that some sequences or source procedures overlap with public benchmark sets (e.g., Cholec80, AutoLaparo). While downstream datasets are established, explicit verification of deduplication between LEMON and the evaluation benchmarks should be discussed.

Backbone capacity and architectural parity in main benchmarks: LemonFM adopts ConvNeXt-L, whereas several compared surgical foundation models (e.g., GSViT, Endo-FM, EndoViT) utilize various Vision Transformer backbones. While Table 5 partially ablates ViT-L vs. ConvNeXt-L on two datasets, explicitly stating the model parameter counts, compute budgets, and backbone configurations across all compared models in Tables 2–4 would better isolate the gains from the pretraining data/method versus architecture size.

Coarse downstream procedure classification: The two proposed video-level classification tasks rely on video title matching (assisted by ChatGPT) and are evaluated at a relatively coarse procedure/surgery type level, which may inherit noise or bias from original YouTube uploader descriptions.

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: LEMON introduces over 4,194 videos (938 hours, 35 procedures), considerably expanding open-access surgical video diversity and volume compared to existing datasets like Cholec80, AutoLaparo, GenSurgery, and SurgeNetXL.

Comprehensive and pragmatic curation pipeline: The multi-stage pipeline specifically addresses the severe noise inherent to web-scraped surgical videos (e.g., out-of-body views, title slides, watermarks, equipment UI/overlays) with quantitative validation of each curation step.

Strong and consistent empirical performance: LemonFM outperforms existing foundation models (Endo-FM, EndoViT, GSViT, SurgeNetXL) across six benchmark datasets and four distinct downstream tasks (phase recognition, tool detection, action recognition, and semantic segmentation) under both linear probing and full fine-tuning.

Thorough ablation studies: The paper systematically evaluates the impact of LEMON pretraining vs. ImageNet, curated vs. uncurated data, the proposed augmented distillation mechanism vs. vanilla DINO, and backbone architectures (ConvNeXt vs. ViT).
weaknesses: Architectural and parameter comparability: LemonFM employs a ConvNeXt-L backbone, while several baseline foundation models use smaller backbones (e.g., ViT-B/16). Although Table 5 includes ConvNeXt-B and ViT-L ablations on two tasks, the main benchmark tables (Tables 2-4) would benefit from explicit reporting of model parameter counts and FLOPs to ensure clear attribution of gains between architecture capacity and dataset quality.

Methodological novelty of pretraining: The augmented distillation strategy adapts DINO by pulling k-NN intra-procedure and temporal adjacent frames into the positive augmentation pool. While intuitive and empirically effective for surgical video, this is a relatively incremental extension of existing retrieval-augmented and temporal contrastive SSL techniques.

YouTube data limitations and distribution shift: Sourcing videos from YouTube introduces severe platform-specific compression artifacts and potential selection bias toward successfully edited or educational procedures. Discussion of how this affects transfer to raw, uncompressed operating room video streams would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Large-scale and diverse dataset contribution: LEMON addresses the significant data scarcity problem in surgical computer vision by compiling 4,194 videos (938 hours across 35 surgical procedures), markedly expanding both the volume and procedural diversity compared to existing open surgical datasets.

Well-engineered curation pipeline: The multi-stage curation strategy (storyboard classification, frame-level trimming, and YOLOv8-based obliteration of non-surgical UI/logos) is practical and demonstrably effective. Ablation experiments (Table 5) clearly validate that removing non-surgical content produces measurable performance gains (+4.5pp F1 in phase recognition, +1.3pp mDice in segmentation).

Thorough downstream evaluation: LemonFM is rigorously benchmarked across six public datasets spanning four distinct clinical tasks (phase recognition, tool presence, action recognition, and semantic segmentation). LemonFM achieves substantial improvements over established surgical foundation models (e.g., Endo-FM, EndoViT, SurgeNetXL) under both frozen linear probing and full fine-tuning protocols.

Domain-appropriate self-supervised pretraining: Augmenting DINO distillation with cross-patient nearest-neighbor frames within the same procedure and adjacent temporal frames is well-motivated for surgical scenes, encouraging invariance to inter-patient anatomical differences and small motion artifacts.
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: The algorithmic components rely heavily on existing frameworks. The pretraining objective is a straightforward modification of DINO incorporating nearest-neighbor retrieval (reminiscent of NNCLR) and temporal sampling, while the video aggregation scheme (LemonFM-Vid) directly adopts typicality weighting from prior active learning literature.

Risk of data leakage and distribution overlap: Because the videos are scraped from YouTube using keyword queries, there is a possibility that clips from widely used public datasets (such as Cholec80 or AutoLaparo) or institutional sources represented in the test sets were re-uploaded to YouTube and incorporated into pretraining. The manuscript does not detail explicit deduplication or near-duplicate detection against downstream test sets.

Lack of temporal pretraining: Although LEMON consists of video data, pretraining is conducted purely as 2D frame-level distillation at 1 fps. While adjacent frames are used as positive pairs, the model does not learn true spatiotemporal dynamics during pretraining, relying instead on downstream heads (e.g., MS-TCN) to model time.

Confounding factors in foundation model comparisons: Baselines in Tables 2–4 vary in both backbone architecture and pretraining token budgets. While Table 5 partially addresses this by comparing ConvNeXt-L with ViT-L, a more controlled comparison matching pretraining steps, batch sizes, and model capacities across pretext objectives would provide clearer insights.

strengths: Substantial and timely dataset contribution: LEMON introduces over 4,100 curated videos across 35 minimally invasive surgical procedures (totaling 938 hours), considerably expanding the scale, procedural diversity, and availability of open-access surgical datasets.

Well-engineered curation pipeline: Sourcing surgical video from the open web introduces substantial noise (lecture slides, patient interviews, equipment logos, and UI overlays). The multi-stage filtering and in-frame content obliteration using storyboard classifiers, frame-level trimming, and YOLOv8 object detection is rigorous and demonstrated to be effective.

Methodologically tailored pretraining: The augmented distillation strategy intuitively and effectively tailors self-supervised learning to surgical video by mining cross-patient nearest neighbors within the same procedure and adjacent temporal frames, enforcing invariance to minor camera/tool motions and inter-patient tissue variations.

Comprehensive downstream benchmarking: The paper conducts rigorous evaluations across six independent benchmarks spanning four distinct downstream tasks (phase recognition, tool presence detection, action recognition, and semantic segmentation) under both linear probing and full fine-tuning regimes, as well as in low-data (50% shot) setups.

Strong and consistent empirical improvements: LemonFM convincingly outperforms prior domain-specific foundation models (e.g., SurgeNetXL, Endo-FM, EndoViT) and task-specific specialists across downstream benchmarks by clear margins.
weaknesses: Long-term reproducibility and YouTube link rot: Sourcing videos via web scraping from YouTube frequently suffers from video deletion, channel takedowns, and regional copyright restrictions over time. While the authors state that academic researchers can request access via LMDB format, reliance on dynamic public web URLs remains a challenge for reproducibility and long-term dataset maintenance.

Ethical and patient consent nuances: Although the authors spent significant human effort removing identifying information and out-of-body views and established an opt-out mechanism, secondary use of clinical procedures scraped from public social media platforms carries inherent ethical gray zones regarding explicit patient consent for machine learning modeling.

Architectural fairness in baseline comparisons: LemonFM is built on ConvNeXt-Large, whereas several compared foundation models (e.g., EndoViT, GSViT) use standard ViT backbones. While Table 6 provides an ablation between ViT-L and ConvNeXt on two tasks, the main comparison tables (Tables 2–4) mix architectural backbones, making it difficult to fully isolate the individual gains attributable to dataset scale, model capacity/inductive bias, and the proposed augmented distillation objective across all benchmarks.

strengths: Substantial dataset scale and clinical diversity: LEMON represents an impactful open-access contribution to surgical computer vision, featuring 4,194 videos spanning 938 hours and 35 distinct procedure types, significantly surpassing existing open datasets in scale and procedural breadth.

Rigorous and multi-stage curation pipeline: The authors address critical issues in web-crawled medical videos by systematically filtering non-surgical videos via storyboards, trimming introductory/concluding slides, and masking intraoperative non-surgical UI/logo artifacts using an object detector, supported by high validation metrics.

Well-motivated domain-specific self-supervised pretraining: The augmented knowledge distillation framework smartly incorporates both cross-patient nearest-neighbor retrieval (for appearance/color variance) and adjacent temporal frame sampling (for motion invariance), showing clear improvements over standard DINO.

Comprehensive downstream benchmarking: Evaluated extensively across six standard surgical benchmarks (AutoLaparo, Cholec80, M2CAI16, GraSP, CholecT50, CholecSeg8k) covering four downstream perception tasks; LemonFM consistently outperforms previous surgical foundation models (e.g., SurgeNetXL, Endo-FM, EndoViT) in both linear probing and full fine-tuning.

Thorough ablation studies and practical efficiency analysis: The paper includes insightful ablations detailing the impact of data scale, data curation, distillation thresholding, and architecture choices (ConvNeXt vs. ViT), alongside runtime latency and memory profiling demonstrating real-time capability.
weaknesses: Dataset longevity and distribution risks: Relying on YouTube video links inherently introduces vulnerability to video takedowns, privacy changes, and link rot over time; while an LMDB distribution upon request is mentioned, sustaining long-term access and reproducibility remains a challenge.

Pretraining temporal density: Pretraining at 1 fps effectively treats the data as disjointed keyframes rather than modeling dense temporal dynamics, which may limit the model's direct applicability to fine-grained kinematic tracking or high-speed instrument motion without external temporal heads (e.g., MSTCN).

Evaluation procedural concentration: Although LEMON curates 35 procedures, downstream fine-grained evaluation tasks (tool presence, phase, segmentation) predominantly concentrate on standard laparoscopy benchmarks like cholecystectomy and hysterectomy, leaving the fine-grained transfer to the rarer curated procedures evaluated mostly via coarse video-level classification.

strengths: Substantial dataset scale and procedural diversity: LEMON introduces 4,194 surgical videos totaling 938 hours across 35 distinct surgical procedures, significantly expanding upon existing open-access surgical vision benchmarks in both scale and clinical breadth.

Well-designed and documented data curation pipeline: The multi-stage curation strategy (storyboard classification, frame-level boundary trimming, intraoperative non-surgical frame elimination, and UI/text bounding-box obliteration via YOLOv8) is systematic, practical, and backed by extensive manual verification (over 100 expert hours).

Domain-specific SSL design: The augmented distillation method tailors the DINO framework to endoscopic video by mining intra-procedure cross-patient nearest neighbors and adjacent temporal frames into the distillation target, encouraging invariance to non-semantic tissue appearance variations and slight motion.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: The proposed foundation model is evaluated across six established public benchmarks and four downstream tasks (phase recognition, tool detection, action recognition, and semantic segmentation) under both linear probing and full fine-tuning protocols, showing consistent and substantial improvements over existing surgical foundation models (e.g., Endo-FM, SurgeNetXL) and specialist baselines.

Thorough ablations: The manuscript provides systematic ablation experiments demonstrating the individual value of large-scale domain data, rigorous data cleaning, the augmented distillation pool, and architectural choices (ConvNeXt vs. ViT).
weaknesses: Limitations of 2D/1 fps pretraining for temporal dynamics: LemonFM is trained purely as an image-level model at 1 fps, delegating video temporal modeling entirely to downstream temporal decoders (e.g., MS-TCN). While the authors demonstrate good real-time inference latency and strong dense downstream performance, natively spatio-temporal representations are not learned during foundation model pretraining.

Web video dataset stability and curation noise: Although common in computer vision, sourcing videos from YouTube introduces potential dataset longevity issues (link rot, takedown requests) and uncontrolled recording/compression quality differences across institutions. While the authors mitigate this with direct LMDB access for academics, long-term dataset maintenance will require sustained effort.

Relatively simplistic video classification head: The proposed downstream video classification model (LemonFM-Vid) relies on a fairly heuristic frame typicality aggregation scheme; while it outperforms baseline video models, further analysis into why certain anatomically related procedures remain confused (57.8% mAP) would strengthen the diagnostic insights.
